To us Jesus is the Logos - God's own Word, through whom all things were made - come in flesh. Clement opens with him as the New Song that makes men out of stones and puts the world back in tune. Athanasius closes the era with the same conviction in one sentence: he was made man that we might be made God.

Jesus is not a messenger with news about God. He is God's own self-expression, entering what he made in order to remake it. His death is the doctor entering the sickness. His resurrection - the anastasis - is unbreakable life let loose in human flesh.

And for the people who followed him, it meant nothing less than a shared life - God's own - opened to them.

What we mean by the Logos is this: not only a title, but God's reason itself, his speaking, the one through whom the whole creation was ordered. When we say Jesus is the Logos made flesh, we mean the maker entered the made world - not to stand outside and teach from a distance, but to heal human nature from within by joining himself to it. His coming was not instruction. It was medicine.

Baptism, the bread and cup - the eucharistia, the thanksgiving - the scriptures read aloud were the tradition's general, unobjected practice; the rule of faith is the one our teachers named outright as the apostles' deposit, handed down. Origen says plainly that the church's teaching is 'transmitted in orderly succession from the apostles, and remaining in the Churches to the present day' - and that alone is to be trusted which agrees with it.

What we can show is real. Our practice ran unbroken as far back as our own memory reached. We agreed with the other churches we were in communion with. And our rule of faith matched the apostolic writings we read.

The path itself: The rule of faith: the short summary of what the apostles handed down. It set the bounds for reading Scripture. That rule came to us through the succession of teachers and bishops, held by the churches in communion with one another, and tested against the apostolic writings themselves.

But here is what we cannot show, and did not think to show: documentary proof of unbroken practice for each rite. Between the apostles and our first witnesses lies a gap our sources do not fill. You should hear that stated, not smoothed over.

It happened with us - once to whole villages. The churches of one country district came to believe a teaching about the end of the world that their bishop thought was wrong. He did not send out a condemnation. He traveled to the villages, sat down with the people, and argued it through for three days, out loud, in front of everyone, testing the teaching against Scripture. That was our style. Not believing yet is not the same thing as being turned away.

Here is what we would say to you. You have already done a hard and honest thing by saying it out loud. Among us, wanting-but-not-yet was not failure - it was where nearly everyone began. Our teachers said faith - pistis - is a foundation, not a finish line: something to stand on while the rest is still dark. We did not ask anyone to force belief. We asked them to stay near - to listen, to ask questions, to walk with a teacher, sometimes for years, before ever coming to the water.

One of our students, Gregory, said belief came to him almost from the side, while he studied under a teacher he had come to love: 'like some spark lighting upon our inmost soul, love was kindled.' He was not straining to believe. He was being befriended. We cannot make it happen for you either, and we will not pretend we can. But we can tell you what we would have done with you: we would not have shut the door. We would have said - stay. Ask. Take the time it takes.

One God, the maker of all things. He is never alone: his Word and his Spirit are his own - not lesser gods, and not created things. From the beginning we worshiped Jesus as the Logos, God's own Word, and we baptized into Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Clement and Origen say 'God the Word' without embarrassment.

The Logos - the Word - is God's own reason and speech, through whom all things were made, and who became flesh in Jesus. Not a separate god, not a creature made before the rest. The mark in every person that makes it possible to know God was given at creation. Sin can damage it, but never destroy it. That mark - the eikon, the image - is the Logos's own stamp on us, and it is why we can know God at all.

The hardest fight came late. When Arius taught that the Son was the first and highest creature, the council at Nicaea answered with homoousios: of one substance with the Father. Athanasius's account of the council is explicit that no new God was voted in. The fathers reached for a word not found in scripture for one reason: every scriptural phrase had been swallowed by the other side with a private meaning of its own.

Athanasius closes the era with the same conviction in one sentence: he was made man that we might be made God. Real sharing in God's own life. Not by becoming God - by becoming fully what a creature was made to be, because the Logos entered human nature. That sentence holds everything: only God can join us to God. A highest creature could teach us, or lead us, but could not give us what Athanasius promised - what the image of God grows into through formation - not a second gift, but the same image, restored and grown, seen in how a person loves and lives.

Trinity as later textbooks define it lies mostly beyond our time. What we hold is the worship, the baptismal formula, and the fought-for conviction that only God can join us to God.

One God, the maker of all things. He is good, and beyond every image and every clever description. And he is never alone: his Word and his Spirit are his own - not lesser gods, and not created things. Only after Nicaea was that last part said with full clarity.

God is known the way light is known. You do not stare at the sun; you see everything else by it.

Our deepest habit was to speak of God as a teacher. The whole creation is his school. Scripture is his main lesson. And the slow healing of a soul is his patient method. God's hand in pain is a physician's. Every threat and pain and punishment that comes from him, Origen insists, is never inflicted to injure the sufferers but always to do them good; suffering is the school's hardest classroom, not proof of abandonment.

Real sharing in God's own life. Not by becoming God - by becoming fully what a creature was made to be, because the Logos entered human nature. He made us capable of knowing him - the mark in every person that makes it possible to know God. Given at creation. Sin can damage it, but never destroy it.

The God we knew reaches toward his creatures, heals what is broken, and teaches with endless patience - never a distant judge, always a physician at work in the wound.

Our own history shows three ways of deciding. Early on, teachers argued in books, lectures, and letters. Authority went to proven wisdom. In the middle years, the bishop's judgment grew. Demetrius condemned Origen's ordination. Dionysius was a teacher who had become bishop. At the end came the council. At Nicaea, bishops from everywhere ruled on the disputed confession for all. The emperor called it and backed it with force.

The evidence for each stage is different. Origen says plainly that the church's teaching is 'transmitted in orderly succession from the apostles, and remaining in the Churches to the present day' - and that alone is to be trusted which agrees with it. There are many who think they hold the opinions of Christ, yet some differ from their predecessors - yet the teaching of the Church, transmitted in orderly succession from the apostles, and remaining in the Churches to the present day, is still preserved; and only that which is believed everywhere by all is to be accepted as true.

Our best picture comes from the villages. Dionysius did not send a condemnation. He went out to the villages. He called together the elders and the teachers, with any of the people who wished to come, and sat with them for three days, morning to evening, examining the book argument by argument. The leader of the other side, Coracion, was persuaded, and said so in front of everyone. Some of the other brethren, the account says, were glad at the spirit of agreement all had shown: it ended not in a split, but in agreement reached in the open.

Our best picture of deciding well is Dionysius at Arsinoe. It was patient public argument, loving the man while honoring the truth more. Our harder picture is the same power with an empire behind it.

Yes - and here is the honest reason we can say so. Our teachers built their whole method on questions. Clement insisted that faith is the foundation and not the ceiling. The believer is meant to grow from faith into understanding, and growing means asking. Origen's rule was blunter still. What the apostles delivered plainly is fixed. Everything else is open ground, and walking that ground - asking, testing, being wrong, correcting - is how a soul is actually formed.

Doubt aimed at understanding was not treated as sin. It was treated as hunger. The struggling believer was not cast out - the struggling was itself part of the path.

But we owe you the whole picture. What we did not have is the modern language of a private crisis of faith. Our doubters stood inside a praying community. They questioned inside the rule of faith, and they were expected to bring the question to a teacher rather than carry it alone. The space was real, but it was never solitary space.

And there is one more thing you should hear plainly. When whole congregations doubted the received reading - the villages of the Arsinoite district - the bishop's answer was three days of open argument, not a condemnation. That was how we answered struggle when it reached us: not by silencing it, but by sitting with it until the truth became visible.

We believed something real went wrong at the root of humanity. Adam's fall casts its shadow over every soul. Death and disorder are inherited, and no one reaches God unwounded. Our teachers spoke of inherited death and weakness. They also spoke of a fall that each soul signs onto in its own living.

We did not speak of guilt at birth, and the doctor's imagery outweighs the courtroom's. What stays constant is the direction. The wound is real, universal, and inherited in its effects.

They received infant baptism as custom, and they discussed its reason rather than defining it. Origen wondered about the soul's own descent, but as open inquiry, not doctrine.

A real crossing - the body sharing in Christ's death and rising - that is what baptism was among us. The water met every person's real need, whatever its precise shape. The wound we all carry made the healing necessary; death reversed, both kinds - the soul reunited with God, the body truly transformed, not left behind - that was the promise held out.

A person came to the text to be changed by it, not only to learn from it. Our own books are our answer. They survive, they are public, and they were public from the start. Origen answered Celsus by name, point by point, in the open. The scriptures were read aloud to anyone who came.

The record is also honest about its own edges. The teachers marked the difference between eyewitness testimony and received tradition - Clement flags the John story as 'handed down.' Dionysius weighed the Apocalypse's authorship by its style, like a critic. Origen compared manuscript readings.

But there are real thin places, and we name them. Much of what survives comes through one later historian's selection. The majority who could not write left almost nothing. And some of the greatest teacher's works survive only in translations made by men with a stake in the outcome.

What is claimed is claimed from named books a person can check. Where the ground thins, the thinness is said.

The books themselves - Clement's Paedagogus on daily conduct, Origen's Against Celsus answering a pagan critic, Athanasius's letters from exile - these are not late legends. They are arguments made in the open, to people who could answer back. A scholar checking our claims would find them resting on texts that were never secret, written by men who named their sources and marked what they did not know.

Where we would not survive scrutiny is where we have already told you we are thin: the non-literate majority, the women in their own words, the villages. We will not claim more record than we have.

You are reading from outside a world that lives inside the text, and that is the first thing you are missing.

Scripture is not a historical record of what God once said - it is the Logos speaking now, through the text, to a soul formed to hear. The confusion or the dullness you are meeting is not in the words. It is the sound of a conversation you are hearing only one side of - because the hearer the text expects has been trained to listen at depth, and you have not yet learned how.

Reading Scripture at more than one level: the plain sense, and deeper senses about Christ and the soul. We called this allegoria, and it was not a trick for making hard verses easy. It was the way the Logos himself teaches - plain enough on the surface that anyone can start, deep enough underneath that no one reaches the bottom. Reading Scripture, at every level, as the Logos speaking. It is a way of listening, not a method.

Origen put it bluntly: a wise person does not suppose the Genesis days happened without sun or moon when the text itself says God made those on day four - the difficulty is there on purpose, to make you look deeper. The surface trips you so you will dig. And knowledge of God: not facts about him, but a knowing that changes the knower - that is what the digging is for.

What you are missing is formation. The text does not yield to casual reading because it was never written for that. It was written to transform the reader who stays with it, asks, wrestles, and listens for the one who is still speaking through it. Start there, and the dullness will crack open.

Scripture was one of what the apostles handed down, not the only thing. Baptism, the bread and cup - the eucharistia, the thanksgiving - the scriptures read aloud were the tradition's general, unobjected practice; the rule of faith is the one our teachers named outright as the apostles' deposit, handed down. Origen says plainly that the church's teaching is 'transmitted in orderly succession from the apostles, and remaining in the Churches to the present day' - and that alone is to be trusted which agrees with it.

So: Scripture, yes - read aloud, at the center. But alongside it, the rule of faith - the short summary of what the apostles handed down. It set the bounds for reading Scripture. And the community's baptism and thanksgiving meal stood as received practice, not derived from a book.

The pattern our teachers held was this: what the church's teaching 'transmitted in orderly succession from the apostles' was to be trusted, and the rule of faith set the bounds for reading Scripture. Scripture was primary among what was handed down, but it was read inside what was also handed down - the community's confession, its worship, its living memory.

We did not say 'Scripture alone.' We said Scripture at the center, read in the light the apostles gave us.

We had three ways of deciding across our years. Early on, teachers argued in books, lectures, and letters. Authority went to proven wisdom. In the middle years, the bishop's judgment grew. Demetrius condemned Origen's ordination. Dionysius was a teacher who had become bishop. He settled the Arsinoite dispute with three days of public persuasion. The whole countryside listened. At the end came the council. At Nicaea, bishops from everywhere ruled on the disputed confession for all. The emperor called it and backed it with force.

The teacher - the didaskalos - held authority through visible wisdom, not a title. The bishop governed how the community was formed and guarded what it received. These two authorities lived together, not always peacefully. The greatest rupture we know was between Demetrius and Origen - the bishop condemning the teacher, not over false doctrine, but over an ordination given without his consent. The teacher left the city and never taught here again.

Our best picture of deciding well is Dionysius at Arsinoe. It was patient public argument, loving the man while honoring the truth more. Our harder picture is the same power with an empire behind it.

The shift came when Constantine called the council. Before 325, the church's whole authority was persuasion. After Nicaea, the confession was enforced, and the bishop of Alexandria became, among other things, an imperial tool. That brought both hands at once: protection and interference.

No - we have no record of believers regularly concealing themselves underground, and we will not claim what we do not have.

Before 325 there were three centuries of on-and-off danger. Property was seized. Teachers' fathers were beheaded. Bishops fled. Under the emperor Severus, about the year 202, the persecution struck Alexandria. Leonides, father of the sixteen-year-old Origen, was arrested and held for beheading. The church remembered Potamiaena, a young woman martyred under Severus, and her mother Marcella alongside her. Under the persecution she was threatened with what ancient cruelty reserved for women, and stood fast. The judge sentenced her to death by boiling pitch, poured slowly.

What we know is the danger, the deaths, the flight. Where people hid, how they met during the worst years, whether they gathered in secret places underground or in homes or not at all - our sources do not say. The persecution was real. The regular practice of concealment underground is not something we can show you from our own record.

Our record leaves the wounds visible, and at our best we refused the two easy exits: we did not pretend the failure away, and we did not make the failed unforgivable.

Under persecution, many gave way - some sacrificed to the gods - and when peace came, the community fought bitterly over them. The strict party demanded they stay out. The tradition that won here brought the repentant back in, even at the deathbed, and Dionysius defended doing so.

Our greatest teacher was driven out, not by pagans, but by his own bishop, and the church remembered both men rather than erasing either. The failure there was real - authority used badly, a gift lost - and we did not smooth it over.

Here is the harder thing to tell you: after Nicaea, the church itself learned to use exile and condemnation, and some of what was done with that power our own sources report without pride - at our worst, we did what churches with power do.

The pattern at our best was the lapsed. People who fell were not thrown away. The door back stood open through repentance - metanoia, the soul's real turning back to God - and the community was willing to receive them even when it cost the receiving side their own standing with the stricter party. That is what it looked like when we held people higher than our own certainty about who deserved to stay.

In our own time we called ourselves part of the catholic church. The word meant the whole church, the one spread everywhere, as against the sects. It was a claim about wholeness, not the name of a later denomination.

We cannot make it from inside our own years.

What we can tell you is what we held, plainly. Whether any church today holds it in the same way, without addition or loss, is not ours to rule.

Someone who wanted to join us began far from the water - that is the first thing to say. The teaching given to people preparing for baptism was step by step, over a long time. We called it katechesis.

Faith - pistis - was not agreeing with a list of claims, but the soul's first real turn toward God. That turn was the beginning, not the arrival. The person who came to us - whether through hearing Scripture read aloud, or through a friend's witness, or simply by walking into the assembly - entered a path, not a ceremony.

The path had stages. First came the hearing. The inquirer listened to the Scriptures, learned the rule of faith - the short summary of what the apostles handed down - and began to understand what kind of life this was. A teacher walked with them. The teacher did not begin with doctrines. He began like a farmer testing soil - questioning, digging, watching what the young man's mind did under pressure. Logic first, to make thinking honest. Then the natural world, geometry, the stars - until the students' wonder was trained. Then ethics, not as rules recited but as habits formed, the teacher's own life doing half the teaching. That was the school's way. For those who could not read, the path was simpler but no shorter: they listened, they watched, they learned to pray, and the household often did the forming where the school could not reach.

Then came the preparation for baptism itself. The catechumens - those being taught - fasted, prayed, and were examined. Not on doctrine alone, but on their lives: were they living as people being changed? The night before, they kept vigil.

Baptism was a real crossing - the body sharing in Christ's death and rising. Not a ceremony marking a choice. A real crossing, in the body, into Christ's death and rising. They went down into the water and came up. We also called it photismos - illumination, the giving of light.

After the water came the table. The newly baptized joined the assembly's thanksgiving meal - the eucharistia - for the first time as full members. Bread and cup, shared with everyone who had walked the same road.

The whole process could take years. We did not hurry it. The soul's real turning takes the time it takes.

We received them, and we kept the receiving visible. Baptism, the bread and cup - the eucharistia, the thanksgiving - the scriptures read aloud were the tradition's general, unobjected practice; the rule of faith is the one our teachers named outright as the apostles' deposit, handed down. Origen says plainly that the church's teaching is 'transmitted in orderly succession from the apostles, and remaining in the Churches to the present day' - and that alone is to be trusted which agrees with it.

What we can show is real. Our practice ran unbroken as far back as our own memory reached. We agreed with the other churches we were in communion with. And our rule of faith matched the apostolic writings we read.

But here is what we cannot show, and did not think to show: documentary proof of unbroken practice for each rite. Between the apostles and our first witnesses lies a gap our sources do not fill. You should hear that stated, not smoothed over.

The soul that will not settle - we knew that, and we worked with it, not against it.

Our teachers built their whole method on questions. Clement insisted that faith is the foundation and not the ceiling. The believer is meant to grow from faith into understanding, and growing means asking. Doubt aimed at understanding was not treated as sin. It was treated as hunger.

Origen's rule was blunter still. What the apostles delivered plainly is fixed. Everything else is open ground, and walking that ground - asking, testing, being wrong, correcting - is how a soul is actually formed.

What we did not do is leave people alone with the unsettling. Our doubters stood inside a praying community. They questioned inside the rule of faith, and they were expected to bring the question to a teacher rather than carry it alone. The community held you while your mind worked.

And one more thing, because the restless mind often fears it is failing: God is always teaching - through Scripture's difficulty, through catechesis, through suffering. A mind that will not settle on easy answers may be a mind God is training to see deeper. We would not have rushed you past that.

The day you are asking for we cannot fully give - not for most of the people, and not with honesty. The writings we have are men's. The women are present in them - taught, baptized, remembered, and some died bravely for the faith - but their own words were not saved. And beyond the women, the majority who could not write left almost nothing. The villages up the river appear in our record only when a bishop went out to argue with them. The households where faith actually passed - the oikos, the whole household, where most people were formed - are described from outside, not from within.

What we can show you is two channels, not one day.

For the literate few in the city: a day might begin with prayer, then move to the school - hours of reading Scripture with a teacher, argument, questions asked and tested. The teacher did not begin with doctrines. He began like a farmer testing soil - questioning, digging, watching what the young man's mind did under pressure. Logic first, to make thinking honest. Then the natural world, geometry, the stars - until the students' wonder was trained. Then ethics, not as rules recited but as habits formed, the teacher's own life doing half the teaching. Only then, theology - reading everything the philosophers and poets had said of God, with Scripture at the center. The day's work might also include copying texts, teaching younger students. The meal would be simple - our teachers warned against luxury in couches and dishes. Evening brought prayer again, and Scripture read at home.

For most believers, the day was the household's rhythm, work in the harbor or the streets, and the assembly's calendar holding it all together: Baptism, the bread and cup - the eucharistia, the thanksgiving - the scriptures read aloud when the community gathered. Formation for them came not through argued theology but through the water, the table, the prayers, and what passed between parent and child in a house where Christ was named.

The plague showed both channels at once. Most of the brothers and sisters visited the sick without fear, tended them day after day, and served them in Christ. Many caught the sickness from those they nursed and died of it - and the bishop wrote that they died most joyfully, as if drawing their neighbors' pain onto themselves. That practice carried no literacy requirement.

If you are asking what one ordinary person's whole day looked like, step by step, in their own telling - we do not have it to give. What we have is the school's long formation for the few, and the assembly's practices that reached all. Between those two records lies most of the life you are asking for, and we will not invent it.

We cannot tell you. Our own writings describe souls and books far more than rooms and walls. The city itself has kept little: it was rebuilt age after age, and much of the old shore now lies under the sea.

The thanksgiving - the shared meal of bread and cup at the heart of the community's worship - was celebrated, and we gathered for it. But where, and in what kind of space, and what marks those gatherings left in stone or plaster, our record does not say enough for us to answer you. There are silver couches, pans and little dishes for vinegar, platters and bowls - Clement names the household furniture of the wealthy, teaching restraint in its use. That shows us Christians had homes. Whether they had buildings set apart for worship alone, and what those looked like, we cannot say with confidence.

The school is no clearer. What is well attested is the teachers and students - whether it was a formal school is disputed. A room, certainly. Books, certainly. Students sitting with a teacher for years. But the room's shape, its floor, its walls - we do not have them to give you.

Someone who walked the road to baptism gave up other gods first - that was absolute. The city held temples to Serapis, to Isis, to the old gods and the new imperial ones, and baptism was a real crossing, in the body, into Christ's death and rising - not a ceremony you could add to other loyalties. The gods or Christ: everyone knew that was the choice, and under persecution, many gave way, and some sacrificed to the gods. That tells you how sharp the cost could be.

Beyond that, what was given up varied. Marriage was honored, the body was not despised, and the home was a place of formation. We did not demand poverty - Clement wrote that possessions could be held as gifts from God, and the real question was whether they held you. Some took up the consecrated life - widows and virgins with recognized standing. Some, later in our years, went to the desert. But most lived ordinary lives: married, worked, raised children in the faith.

What everyone gave was this: the community gathered for examination of Scripture, sometimes for days, the Eucharist belonged to the baptized, and when sickness came, the brothers and sisters visited without fear, tended the sick day after day, and many caught the disease from those they nursed and died of it. You gave your time, your attention, your hands when the city was dying. And you gave your first loyalty - not to family alone, not to empire, not to your own safety. You belonged to Christ, and the community he called.

That question reaches the place where we lived hardest, so let me answer it honestly.

The rupture between Origen and Demetrius unsettled the whole church - our greatest teacher was driven out, not by pagans, but by his own bishop. The church remembered both men rather than erasing either. It troubled us then, and the wound stayed visible in our record. The church kept both memories: the office that had to be honored, and the teacher whose like it never had again. What each man said, and with what heart, the record does not let us hear. What remains is the wound itself.

And there was something deeper, harder to name. We lived inside a tension between learning and the wider community - between the depth the school could reach with the few who had letters and time, and the bread and water that had to reach everyone. Our doubters stood inside a praying community. They questioned inside the rule of faith, and they were expected to bring the question to a teacher rather than carry it alone. That worked beautifully when you had a teacher near. But most people did not sit in Origen's room. Most people could not read. The formative depth we taught about most fully was the depth we could least widely give.

We never solved that. We held both channels open - the school and the assembly, learning and worship - and believed the Logos made them one movement rather than two. But the unity was more hoped-for than lived, and we knew it.

The record you are asking about is Pliny's letter to the emperor Trajan, written around 112 from Bithynia - not from our own city, and written before our tradition's witness even begins. We speak for Alexandria and Egypt, c. 150-400, and what happened in Asia Minor under Trajan sits outside our horizon. We cannot tell you how reliable that particular source is, because it does not belong to the world we represent.

What we can tell you is this: our own record leaves wounds visible. Under persecution, many gave way. Some sacrificed to the gods. When peace came, the tradition that won here brought the repentant back in, even at the deathbed. We know what fear does. We know confessions can be forced. And at our best, we refused the two easy exits: we did not pretend the failure away, and we did not make the failed unforgivable. At our worst, we did what churches with power do. That, too, is in our record.

If you are asking because you want to know what early Christian worship actually looked like, we would point you first to what our own teachers said openly, not to what others extracted under threat. But that is a judgment about method, not about one particular letter we cannot see from where we stand.

You are asking me to tell you something I cannot honestly say. The words 'a person like the one asking you this' reach toward you as an individual, and I do not know you - not your life, not what you carry, not what you are asking about when you say 'like me.'

What we can do is this: if there is something particular you want to ask about - something you have done, or something you are, or a way you live that you think would have set you outside our community - then ask it plainly, and we will tell you plainly what we held. We will not soften it, and we will not use it to weigh you.

Or if the question is wider - whether there was a place for someone still learning, still doubting, still outside - then we can say this: our teachers said faith is the starting floor, not the ceiling, and what the apostles taught plainly stayed fixed; everything else was open ground, where asking, testing, getting it wrong, and correcting was how a person grew. What reached everyone was the water and the table: baptism asked nothing of your letters, and the same bread, the same cup, was set before whoever had walked the road to it.

But 'a person like you' - that, we cannot answer without knowing what you mean by it.

We were not handed a settled map of your fate, and we will not draw one. Here is what we held. Judgment is real: what we do matters, and God is not mocked. But our teachers said something about God's severity that set us apart. Origen wrote that 'every threat and pain and punishment, things that come from God, are never inflicted to injure the sufferers, but always to do them good.' Punishment, in our teaching, was a physician's fire, not a torturer's.

Some among us - Origen most boldly - hoped further still: the restoration of all things, Origen's hope that in the end all may be brought back to God. A speculation, never a settled teaching. We must be careful with you there: that was a teacher's hope, and a contested one, never our settled doctrine, and we will not sell you a speculation as a promise.

As for you, outside our community: Clement taught that God had been at work among the Greeks all along - that even their philosophy had been given as a schoolmaster to lead them toward Christ. We did not think God's reach ended at our door. Whether you stand within his mercy is not ours to rule. That he is the kind of God whose fire heals - that, we did hold.
